title: Kids Across America Turned Big Questions Into Podcasts
summary:
What does "home" really mean? Was Andy Warhol secretly a woman named Patricia? Kids across America asked questions like these — then turned them into podcasts.

This year, NPR's Student Podcast Challenge received nearly 1,500 podcasts from students in 42 states and Washington, D.C. It's the contest's eighth year. Judges spent the whole summer listening to every single one.

One middle schooler in Brooklyn made a podcast about meeting writer Pat Hackett, who worked for the famous artist Andy Warhol. A fifth-grade class in Hewlett, New York, asked each other: "What do you really know about our country?" — perfect for America's 250th birthday. A middle schooler in Iowa named Kate made a podcast about her Grandpa Ted and the dementia that took him from her. And a student in New York talked about growing up with dyslexia.

Big themes this year? Technology in school — like AI and phone bans. Memory — why some things stick and others fade. And learning from older people, including tough talks about grief.

Next, judges pick the grand prize winners. Those podcasts will air on NPR shows like Morning Edition. Not bad for a school project!
why_it_matters: It shows kids that their own questions and stories are worth sharing, and that a school project can reach a real audience far beyond the classroom.

keywords.explanation: A recorded audio show that you can listen to any time, made of talking, stories, and sounds.
A brain illness that makes it hard for older people to remember things and think clearly.
A learning difference that makes reading and spelling harder for some kids, even when they are smart.
Rules that say phones are not allowed in a place, like a school.
Deep sadness, especially after someone you love dies.
A famous American artist known for bright, repeated paintings of things like soup cans and famous faces.

background_read: NPR (National Public Radio) is a big American radio and news group that makes shows like Morning Edition, which people all over the country listen to.
A podcast is like a radio show you can play whenever you want, and anyone with a phone or computer can make one — which is why schools use them for projects.
The Student Podcast Challenge has been running for eight years, and each year judges listen to every single entry before picking the grand prize winners.
Article_Structure: WHO: Students from 42 states and Washington, D.C., including a middle schooler in Brooklyn, a fifth-grade class in Hewlett, New York, Kate from Iowa, and a student in New York with dyslexia.
WHAT: They made nearly 1,500 podcasts and entered NPR's Student Podcast Challenge in its eighth year.
WHERE: All across America — the contest is run by NPR, and winning podcasts air on NPR shows like Morning Edition.
WHY: Kids turned big personal questions about home, memory, family, and reading struggles into real audio stories people will hear.

perspectives.description: Fans of the contest say it proves kids can tackle serious topics like grief and dementia with honesty and creativity.
Some might ask whether every school has the microphones, computers, and free time to make a podcast, so the contest could favor students with more resources.
Teachers often say that making a podcast teaches research, writing, and speaking all at once — and that students work harder when they know someone besides the teacher will hear it.
